title: A spectral proof of ergodicity for the non-reversible TCP window-size process
locator: Open question 1 (Spectral proof of ergodicity), PDF p. 5
statement: For the piecewise-deterministic Markov process X modelling the TCP window size (linear growth at unit rate, multiplicative jumps by a factor 1/2 at a state-dependent rate), the generator L has an explicit polynomial eigenbasis and the invariant law's moments satisfy m_n(t)' = n m_{n-1}(t) + (2^{-n} - 1) m_n(t); the polynomials are dense in L^2(mu) but the eigenvectors of L are not orthogonal there (for instance the integral of P_1 P_2 against mu is -64/27). Despite the lack of reversibility, is it possible to use the spectral properties of L to get estimates on the long-time behaviour of X?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 for spectral methods and convergence rates for the TCP window-size PDMP and for non-reversible PDMPs generally. The hypocoercivity line (Villani; Dolbeault-Mouhot-Schmeiser) and the Wasserstein/coupling results for this process are what the literature offers; no spectral proof of the ergodicity rate for this specific non-self-adjoint generator was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Ask what 'spectral estimate' can mean for a generator whose eigenvectors are complete but not orthogonal, and test the natural substitute: a Riesz-basis or a similarity-transform bound.
attempt.result: The obstruction is quantitative and can be located exactly. If the polynomial eigenfunctions {P_n} formed a Riesz basis of L^2(mu), the semigroup would satisfy ||P_t f - mu(f)|| <= kappa exp(-lambda_1 t) ||f - mu(f)|| with kappa the Riesz constant, which is the condition number of the change of basis from {P_n} to an orthonormal basis. So the whole question is whether that condition number is finite - and the source's own datum, that the Gram matrix of the P_n has nonzero off-diagonal entries, does not by itself decide this: a basis can be non-orthogonal and still Riesz. What decides it is the growth of the Gram matrix's condition number as the truncation size grows. That is a computable question about a moment matrix determined by the explicit moments m_n, and it is a sharper target than 'use the spectral properties'. It is a reformulation and not a bound: no growth rate is established here.
attempt.obstruction: The eigenvalues are lambda_n = 1 - 2^{-n}, which accumulate at 1; the spectral gap is therefore fine, but the eigenvalue spacing shrinks geometrically, which is exactly the regime in which non-normal operators have large pseudospectra and the naive spectral bound fails by a factor growing with the truncation. For such generators the semigroup can grow transiently by a factor that swamps the exponential decay for a long time, so a spectral bound without control of the Riesz constant says nothing about finite times, which is what an ergodicity estimate is for.
attempt.key_identity: For a complete non-orthogonal eigenbasis the semigroup bound carries the Riesz constant of the basis as a prefactor, and that constant is the limit of the condition numbers of the Gram matrices of the eigenpolynomials under mu - a computable moment problem here, since the moments m_n are explicit.

title: Shape of the instability domain for a two-matrix switched linear system
locator: Open question 2 (Shape of the instability domain) and Conjecture 4.3, PDF p. 10
statement: For the switched linear system dX/dt = A_{I_t} X with I_t a two-state Markov jump process of rate r and A_0, A_1 two fixed 2x2 matrices, let G(r) be the associated top Lyapunov-type functional. Prove Conjecture 4.3: there exists r_c approximately 4.6 such that G'(r) > 0 for r < r_c and G'(r) < 0 for r > r_c, with G(r_c) approximately 0.2, and G(r) -> 0 both as r -> 0 and as r -> infinity. This would imply that the instability set U_alpha = {r > 0 : G(r) > alpha} is empty for alpha > G(r_c) and a nonempty interval for alpha < G(r_c).
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on Lyapunov exponents of two-dimensional Markov-switched linear systems and the shape of the instability domain in the jump rate. Found the general theory (Bene-Chevallier and successors on PDMP Lyapunov exponents) but no proof of unimodality in r for this example. Kept open.

attempt.method: Check the two endpoint claims separately from the unimodality claim, since they have different proofs and different difficulty.
attempt.result: The two limits are the soft part and follow from averaging at both ends: as r -> infinity the switching averages and the system converges to dX/dt = ((A_0+A_1)/2) X, whose exponent is that of the averaged matrix, and as r -> 0 the process spends long stretches in a single matrix, so the exponent converges to the average of the two individual exponents. The conjecture's G(r) -> 0 at both ends is therefore the statement that the averaged matrix and both individual matrices are stable, which is a check on A_0 and A_1, not a limit theorem. The hard and genuinely open part is the strict unimodality in between - a single sign change of G' - and it is worth recording that unimodality is strictly stronger than the existence of a maximum, which follows from continuity plus the two limits. So the honest decomposition is: existence of an interior maximum is free from the endpoints; uniqueness of the critical point is the whole problem.
attempt.obstruction: G(r) is the top Lyapunov exponent of a random product, which has no closed form and is not known to be even differentiable in r for general pairs (A_0, A_1) - Furstenberg-type formulas give it as an integral of a cocycle against the stationary measure of the induced process on the projective line, and that stationary measure moves with r in a way that is only Holder. Establishing a single sign change of the derivative would need monotonicity of that projective stationary measure in r, and no such monotonicity is known.
attempt.key_identity: G(r) tends to the exponent of the averaged matrix (A_0+A_1)/2 as r -> infinity and to the mean of the two individual exponents as r -> 0, so an interior maximum is free from continuity; unimodality is the entire content of the conjecture.

title: Can the instability set in the jump rate be a union of several intervals?
locator: Open question 3 (Oscillations of the Lyapunov exponent), PDF p. 10
statement: Is it possible to choose the two 2x2 matrices A_0 and A_1 in such a way that the set of jump rates r for which the associated switched linear process is unstable is the union of several intervals?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on non-monotone dependence of the top Lyapunov exponent on the switching rate. Found examples of non-monotonicity (a single interior maximum) but no example producing two or more disjoint instability intervals. Kept open.

attempt.method: This is an existence question, so ask what mechanism could produce two disjoint intervals, and whether 2x2 real matrices have enough freedom to supply it.
attempt.result: Two disjoint intervals require G(r) - alpha to change sign four times, hence G to have at least two interior local maxima. In the 2x2 case the projective dynamics lives on the circle RP^1, and the switched flow is a random dynamical system on a one-dimensional compact space; the exponent is the integral of a fixed cocycle against a stationary measure that interpolates between the r -> 0 measure (a mixture of the two deterministic invariant measures) and the r -> infinity measure (the invariant measure of the averaged flow). A second local maximum requires this one-parameter family of measures on the circle to double back, i.e. the family cannot be a monotone interpolation. That is possible in principle - two rotation-like matrices with different rotation numbers produce a resonance structure in r - so the natural construction to try is a pair A_0, A_1 whose projective flows are rotations of incommensurate speeds plus small shear. This is a proposed construction, not a verified example: no pair is exhibited here.
attempt.obstruction: The candidate mechanism is a resonance, and resonances in random switching are typically smoothed: the exponential holding times spread the switching phase uniformly and destroy the locking that would produce a second peak. Making the peak survive needs a nearly deterministic switching schedule, which the exponential clock forbids. Any construction must therefore create the second maximum from the shear rather than the rotation, and the shear contribution to the exponent is monotone in r for the examples in the source.
attempt.key_identity: Two disjoint instability intervals require two interior local maxima of the Lyapunov exponent as a function of the jump rate; the exponent is the integral of a fixed cocycle against the r-dependent stationary measure on RP^1, so the question is whether that one-parameter family of measures can double back.

title: Smoothness of the invariant density of piecewise deterministic Markov processes
statement: What can be said on the smoothness of the density of the invariant measure of such processes (the switched-flow piecewise deterministic Markov processes considered in the paper, including the switched linear systems of Section 4)?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on regularity of invariant densities of PDMPs and of switched linear systems (Bakhtin-Hurth, Bene-Chevallier-Nyquist and successors). Regularity results exist under Hormander-type bracket conditions on the vector fields; the source's examples include ones where the vector fields are collinear on a nontrivial set (the source computes exactly the set where A_0 x and A_1 x are collinear), which is where the bracket condition fails. No general answer found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Read the source's own computation as the answer's shape. It computes Q(x) = det(A_0 x, A_1 x) = -y^2 - yz - alpha z^2 and identifies the two lines through the origin where A_0 x and A_1 x are collinear.
attempt.result: That determinant is the bracket condition made explicit, and it says where regularity can and cannot come for free: off the two lines {Q = 0} the pair (A_0 x, A_1 x) spans the plane, the switched flow satisfies a Hormander-type condition and the invariant density can be expected to be smooth by the standard hypoellipticity route for PDMPs; on the two lines the two drifts are parallel and the smoothing mechanism degenerates. So the honest prediction is not 'the density is smooth' but 'the density is smooth off a finite union of lines through the origin, with the behaviour ON those lines being the real question' - and the source's own algebra already tells one where they are. Explicitly, the two lines are y = lambda_+ z and y = lambda_- z with lambda_pm = (1 pm sqrt(1+4alpha))/(2 alpha), which the source computes for a different purpose. This is a localisation of the question, not a regularity theorem.
attempt.obstruction: On the degeneracy lines the invariant measure of a switched flow typically develops a power-law singularity whose exponent is a ratio of the jump rate to the local expansion rate, and that exponent can be less than 1, in which case the density is unbounded and no smoothing argument applies at all. Which side of that threshold the model sits on depends on the pair (r, A_0, A_1) jointly, so there is no dichotomy statement valid for all PDMPs of this class, and a general answer to the question as posed is unlikely to exist.
attempt.key_identity: det(A_0 x, A_1 x) = 0 is exactly the set where the two drift fields are collinear and the bracket condition degenerates; the source computes it as -y^2 - yz - alpha z^2 = 0, a pair of lines through the origin.

title: Convergence to equilibrium for time-reversed PDMPs with unstable fields and unbounded jump rates
statement: Theorem 4.10 of the paper applies to the processes of Examples 4.6 and 4.7. The associated time-reversal processes are associated to unstable vector fields and unbounded jump rates. What can be said about their convergence to equilibrium?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on convergence to equilibrium for PDMPs with unbounded jump rates and expanding flows. The Meyn-Tweedie Lyapunov route and the Wasserstein contraction route both assume either a confining drift or bounded rates; results covering an expanding field with rate growing without bound were not found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Test the two standard machines against the two hypotheses that the question deliberately combines: an expanding vector field, and a jump rate that grows without bound.
attempt.result: They do not fail for the same reason, and separating them is the useful output. A Wasserstein contraction argument fails on the expanding field alone: the flow separates two coupled copies at rate given by the field's positive exponent, and jumps must beat that, which they can only do if the jump kernel is contracting at a rate exceeding the expansion - a condition on the pair, not on either. A Lyapunov (Meyn-Tweedie) argument, by contrast, is actually HELPED by an unbounded jump rate: with rate lambda(x) -> infinity as |x| -> infinity, the generator applied to a test function V growing at infinity acquires a strongly negative term lambda(x)(EV(jump) - V(x)) far out, which dominates the expansion of the field if lambda grows faster than the field's linear rate. So the honest reading is that the two hypotheses push in opposite directions, and the tractable regime is precisely lambda(x) growing superlinearly, where a Lyapunov function should exist. What is not claimed: no drift condition is verified here for the source's Examples 4.6 and 4.7.
attempt.obstruction: A Lyapunov drift condition gives exponential ergodicity only with a small-set/minorisation condition, and for a time-reversed PDMP the natural small set is a compact region that the reversed flow may leave in finite time without a jump, so the minorisation has to come from the jump kernel alone. With an unbounded rate the process also risks explosion in the reversed direction: infinitely many jumps in finite time, which the forward process avoided by construction but the reversal need not.
attempt.key_identity: For a PDMP with generator Lf = F.grad f + lambda(x)(Kf - f), a Lyapunov function needs lambda(x) times the jump decrease to beat F.grad V; an unbounded rate helps this inequality and an expanding field hurts it, so the two hypotheses in the question act in opposite directions.

title: Quantitative convergence for realistic three-dimensional models of bacterial movement
locator: Open question 6 (More realistic models), PDF p. 16
statement: Is it possible to establish quantitative estimates for the convergence to equilibrium for more realistic run-and-tumble dynamics, especially in R^3, as considered in the kinetic and biological literature the paper cites?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on quantitative hypocoercivity for run-and-tumble / velocity-jump processes in three dimensions. There is a substantial post-2014 literature (Dolbeault-Mouhot-Schmeiser style hypocoercivity applied to kinetic transport with a tumbling operator, and Wasserstein/coupling results for the telegraph process) that gives quantitative rates in some three-dimensional settings; I did not verify which of the source's cited models are covered. This row is admitted with that lead recorded, and a merger should check whether the specific models of the source's references are now covered before treating it as fully open.

attempt.method: Ask what is genuinely three-dimensional about the difficulty, since the one-dimensional telegraph process has sharp rates by coupling.
attempt.result: The difficulty is not dimension per se but the geometry of the velocity space. In one dimension the velocity takes two values and a coupling can be built by making the two copies' velocities agree after a single common tumble; in R^3 the velocity lives on the sphere, tumbles are drawn from a kernel on S^2, and two copies at different positions must be brought to the same velocity AND the same position, which a single tumble cannot do. The right substitute is a hypocoercivity estimate in a weighted H^1-type norm on position-velocity space, where the mixing comes from the commutator of the transport operator with the tumbling operator. This says the tractable structural hypothesis is a spectral gap for the tumbling kernel on S^2 plus a confining external field, and identifies which of the source's 'more realistic' features (a chemotactic tumbling rate depending on the gradient along the path) breaks it: a path-dependent rate makes the process non-Markov in (position, velocity) alone and no operator formulation is available.
attempt.obstruction: Realistic chemotaxis models make the tumbling rate depend on the time derivative of the chemoattractant concentration along the trajectory, which adds an internal memory variable. The resulting process is Markov only on an enlarged state space, and on that space the tumbling operator no longer has a spectral gap in the memory direction, so the hypocoercivity commutator argument has nothing to work with in that coordinate.
attempt.key_identity: For run-and-tumble in R^3 the mixing comes from the commutator of v.grad_x with the tumbling operator on S^2; a spectral gap for the tumbling kernel plus a confining field is what makes it quantitative, and a path-dependent (memory) tumbling rate destroys the gap in the memory coordinate.

title: Does Hunt's hypothesis for every proper-subspace projection imply it for the process?
statement: Let X be an R^n-valued Levy process. If for every nonempty proper subspace A of R^n the projection process X_A of X on A satisfies Hunt's hypothesis (H) (every semipolar set is polar), does X itself satisfy (H)?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on Hunt's hypothesis and Getoor's conjecture after 2019, including the Hu-Sun line of work. Getoor's conjecture (essentially all Levy processes satisfy (H)) is described in this 2019 survey as a major unsolved problem and I found no announcement of its resolution; the projection questions of Section 3.2 do not appear to have been answered. Kept open.

attempt.method: Fix the direction that is free. The source's Lemma 3.1 gives the easy implication: if some projection fails (H) then X fails (H). The question is the converse, so ask whether polarity for X can be detected from polarity for all projections.
attempt.result: It cannot, at the level of the underlying capacity theory, and that is the relevant warning. Polarity for a Levy process is an energy condition against the kernel Re[(alpha + psi(z))^{-1}] (the source's own alpha-energy), and the projected process has exponent psi restricted to the subspace, so the projected energy integrates over a lower-dimensional slice of z-space. A set can be non-polar for X (positive capacity) while every projection is polar, and conversely, for the same reason that a compact set in the plane can have positive Hausdorff dimension while its projections in a family of directions are null - the projection of a measure controls only the slice of its Fourier transform along that direction. So the honest content of Question 1 is not 'can projections see polarity' (they cannot in general) but the weaker 'can projections see the semipolar-versus-polar DICHOTOMY', which is a statement about the structure of the exponent rather than about individual sets. Recording that distinction is the useful step; it does not answer the question.
attempt.obstruction: The dichotomy is controlled by how Im(psi) is dominated by 1 + Re(psi) (Kanda-Forst, Rao, and the survey's own C_log conditions). Restricting psi to a subspace can only make the domination easier, since both parts are restricted together, so good behaviour of every restriction is strictly weaker information than good behaviour of psi - there are directions in z-space (not aligned with any subspace restriction in a useful way) along which Im(psi) could escape. Constructing such an exponent, or showing none exists, is the actual work.
attempt.key_identity: Polarity is an energy condition against Re[(alpha + psi(z))^{-1}] over all of z-space; a subspace projection integrates only a slice of that kernel, so the family of projections is strictly less information than the full exponent.

title: Does Hunt's hypothesis for every one-dimensional projection imply it for the process?
statement: Let X be an R^n-valued Levy process. If for every one-dimensional subspace A of R^n the projection process X_A satisfies Hunt's hypothesis (H), does X satisfy (H)?
status_search: Same search as E0022. The survey's own Section 3.2.1 answers the WEAKER Question 3 (coordinate axes only) in the negative by an explicit counterexample; Question 2, which quantifies over ALL one-dimensional subspaces, is left open there and I found no later resolution. Kept open.

attempt.method: Take the source's counterexample to Question 3 and ask how far it can be pushed, since Question 2 differs from Question 3 only by enlarging the family of directions tested.
attempt.result: The counterexample is X_t = a t + sqrt(Q) B_t with Q = [[2,2],[2,2]] and a = (1,-1): each coordinate-axis projection has a nondegenerate Gaussian part and so satisfies (H), but the projection onto the line {y = -x} is a uniform motion, which fails (H), and hence X fails (H) by Lemma 3.1. This shows the mechanism precisely: the failure is a DEGENERATE DIRECTION, a line on which the Gaussian part vanishes and only a drift survives. Question 2 forbids exactly that, since it tests every line including the degenerate one. So Question 2 has content only for processes with no degenerate direction of uniform-motion type, and for the Gaussian-plus-drift family it is therefore TRUE by Theorem 2.5 of the same survey (nondegenerate Q implies (H)). The residual open case is the purely non-Gaussian one, where 'degenerate direction' is not visible from Q. That reduction is the useful output.
attempt.obstruction: For a pure-jump process there is no matrix Q whose rank identifies the bad directions; the analogue is the set of directions in which the Levy measure's projection has finite variation and the projected process is a drift plus a compound Poisson process. Whether that set can be empty in every direction while (H) still fails for X is exactly the open case, and no invariant of the Levy measure is known that detects it.
attempt.key_identity: The survey's counterexample fails (H) through a single degenerate line on which the process becomes uniform motion; quantifying over all lines removes that mechanism, leaving only the pure-jump case as genuinely open.

title: Hunt's hypothesis for a product of two independent Levy processes
statement: Let X_1 and X_2 be independent Levy processes on R^n and R^m respectively, both satisfying Hunt's hypothesis (H). Does the R^{n+m}-valued Levy process X = (X_1, X_2) satisfy (H)? Equivalently (Question 4): if S is a nonempty proper subspace of R^n and the projections X_S and X_{S-perp} are independent and both satisfy (H), does X satisfy (H)?
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 as for E0022; no resolution found. The survey itself proves the special case Proposition 3.10 (if both X_1 and X_2 satisfy its solution condition (S) then the product satisfies (H)), via the additivity of the exponents and the Kanda-Forst condition. Kept open.

attempt.method: Push the survey's own Proposition 3.10 mechanism as far as it goes. The exponent of the product is psi(z_1, z_2) = psi_1(z_1) + psi_2(z_2), so Re and Im are additive; ask which of the known sufficient conditions for (H) is stable under that addition.
attempt.result: Kanda-Forst is stable, which is what Proposition 3.10 uses, and so is Rao's strictly larger class, which the survey does not observe. Rao's condition is |Im(psi)| <= (1 + Re(psi)) f(1 + Re(psi)) with f increasing on [1, infinity) and the integral of 1/(lambda f(lambda)) divergent. If psi_1 and psi_2 both satisfy it with the same f, then using 1 + Re(psi_i) <= 1 + Re(psi) and monotonicity of f, |Im psi| <= |Im psi_1| + |Im psi_2| <= (2 + Re psi_1 + Re psi_2) f(1 + Re psi) <= 2 (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi), so psi satisfies Rao's condition with f replaced by 2f, and the divergence of the integral of 1/(2 lambda f(lambda)) is unaffected. Resolvent densities pass to the product because a convolution with a density is a density. Hence: the answer to Question 4 is YES for every pair of processes in Rao's class. This is a genuine extension of Proposition 3.10 and it is easy; it is emphatically NOT an answer to the question as posed, because the survey's whole point (its Theorems 2.8, 2.11, 2.12) is that (H) holds for processes outside Rao's class.
attempt.obstruction: The survey's weaker sufficient conditions (EKFR, C_log, C_log-log) are quantified over finite measures of finite 1-energy, with a measure-dependent sequence y_k. Under addition of exponents the level sets {y_k <= B(z) < y_k^beta} of B = 1 + Re(psi) change shape in the product space, and a measure on R^{n+m} of finite energy need not factor, so there is no way to produce the required sequence for the product from the two given sequences. That is exactly where the additivity argument stops.
attempt.key_identity: psi_{(X_1,X_2)}(z_1,z_2) = psi_1(z_1) + psi_2(z_2): Re adds and |Im| is subadditive, so any sufficient condition of the form |Im psi| <= (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi) with f increasing survives the sum up to replacing f by 2f.

title: Hunt's hypothesis for pure jump subordinators with infinite Levy measure
statement: Does any pure jump subordinator with infinite Levy measure satisfy Hunt's hypothesis (H)? More generally, does any pure jump n-dimensional Levy process satisfy (H)? The survey records in Section 2 that it is still unknown whether any pure jump subordinator of type-(alpha, beta) satisfies (H), where a pure jump subordinator is of type-(alpha, beta) with 0 < alpha < beta < 1 if its Levy measure has a density nu with c^{-1} x^{-(1+alpha)} <= nu(x) <= c x^{-(1+beta)} for x in (0,1].
status_search: WebSearch 2026-09-08 on Hunt's hypothesis for subordinators after 2019. The survey's own Theorem 2.29 gives (H) for a subclass of type-(alpha,beta) subordinators under an extra condition; no later paper covering all pure jump subordinators with infinite Levy measure was found. Kept open.

attempt.method: Compute the shape of the exponent for a subordinator and see what the Kanda-Forst ratio looks like, since that ratio is the only quantity all the known sufficient conditions control.
attempt.result: For a driftless subordinator the exponent is psi(z) = integral over (0, infinity) of (1 - e^{i z x}) nu(dx), so Re psi(z) = integral (1 - cos(zx)) nu(dx) and Im psi(z) = -integral sin(zx) nu(dx). Both integrands are supported on the same scales, and for a stable-like nu(dx) = x^{-(1+alpha)} dx a scaling computation gives Re psi(z) asymptotically c_alpha |z|^alpha and Im psi(z) asymptotically c_alpha tan(pi alpha / 2) |z|^alpha, so the ratio |Im psi| / (1 + Re psi) is BOUNDED and Kanda-Forst holds - which is why all stable subordinators satisfy (H). The type-(alpha,beta) case is exactly the case where the two-sided bound allows the mass to oscillate between the two scaling exponents, so Re psi can dip along a sparse sequence of z while Im psi does not, and the ratio can be unbounded. This identifies the mechanism precisely: the difficulty is not infinite activity, it is a Levy density with oscillating scaling, and a subordinator whose density has a genuine limit exponent is in Kanda-Forst and hence satisfies (H). This is a description of where the open case lives; it does not settle it.
attempt.obstruction: To exploit the oscillation one has to control Re psi from below along the sparse sequence where Im psi is large, and the two-sided bound c^{-1} x^{-(1+alpha)} <= nu <= c x^{-(1+beta)} does not force Re psi to be regularly varying, so no Tauberian theorem applies. The survey's own weaker conditions require choosing a sequence y_k adapted to each measure of finite energy, which is why Theorem 2.29 covers only a subclass.
attempt.key_identity: For a driftless subordinator with stable density of index alpha, Im psi / Re psi tends to tan(pi alpha / 2), a finite constant - Kanda-Forst holds; the type-(alpha,beta) class is precisely the class where that ratio need not have a limit.

title: Hunt's hypothesis for one-dimensional Levy processes of infinite variation of jumps
statement: Does any one-dimensional Levy process X with integral of (1 and |x|) against nu(dx) equal to infinity satisfy Hunt's hypothesis (H)? The survey notes (Remark 5.1(i), citing Kesten) that a positive answer to Question 7 would imply a positive answer to Question 6.
status_search: Same search as E0025. Kept open.

attempt.method: Use the survey's own reduction (Question 7 implies Question 6, via Kesten's Theorem 1(f)) together with a stability observation for Rao's class.
attempt.result: Combining the two gives a concrete class in which Question 6 has a positive answer. By the argument recorded in E0024, Rao's sufficient condition |Im psi| <= (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi) with f increasing and the integral of 1/(lambda f(lambda)) divergent is stable under independent sums up to replacing f by 2f. Hence any one-dimensional Levy process that DECOMPOSES as an independent sum of processes each in Rao's class is itself in Rao's class and satisfies (H). Since a process with infinite jump variation can always be split at a scale into a small-jump part and a large-jump (compound Poisson) part, and compound Poisson processes have bounded exponent hence trivially satisfy Kanda-Forst, the question reduces to the SMALL-JUMP part alone: Question 6 holds whenever the small-jump component satisfies Rao's condition. That is a genuine reduction (the large-jump part is never the obstruction), and it is not an answer, since the small-jump part is exactly where an oscillating Levy density can break the ratio.
attempt.obstruction: The reduction is only as good as Rao's condition, and the survey's own point is that (H) can hold outside it; conversely the infinite-variation hypothesis in Question 6 does not by itself force any lower bound on Re psi, so it does not force the ratio to be bounded. Getoor's conjecture, which subsumes this question, has been open for fifty years.
attempt.key_identity: Splitting a Levy process at a jump scale writes it as an independent sum of a small-jump part and a compound Poisson part; the latter has bounded exponent and satisfies Kanda-Forst, and Rao's class is closed under independent sums, so only the small-jump part can obstruct (H).

title: Is Hunt's hypothesis stable under independent sums of Levy processes?
statement: Suppose X and Y are two independent n-dimensional Levy processes both satisfying Hunt's hypothesis (H). Does X + Y satisfy (H)?
status_search: Same search as E0025. The survey states this as an open question it has raised before, and records that a positive answer would imply a positive answer to Question 6 by Kesten's Theorem 1(f). Kept open.

attempt.method: Test each of the known sufficient conditions for (H) for stability under addition of the Levy-Khintchine exponents, since psi_{X+Y} = psi_X + psi_Y for independent summands.
attempt.result: Kanda-Forst is stable: if |Im psi_X| <= M(1 + Re psi_X) and |Im psi_Y| <= M(1 + Re psi_Y) then |Im psi| <= M(2 + Re psi_X + Re psi_Y) <= 2M(1 + Re psi). Rao's condition is also stable, with the same argument as in E0024: monotonicity of f and 1 + Re psi_i <= 1 + Re psi give |Im psi| <= 2(1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi), and the required divergence of the integral of 1/(lambda f(lambda)) is unaffected by the factor 2; the sum has resolvent densities as soon as one summand does. So the answer to Question 7 is YES whenever both summands lie in Rao's class - a class strictly larger than Kanda-Forst and containing all stable processes and every process with a nondegenerate Gaussian part. The survey does not record this. The caveat matters and is the reason this is not an answer: the survey's Theorems 2.8, 2.11 and 2.12 exist precisely because (H) holds for processes OUTSIDE Rao's class, and for those the argument gives nothing.
attempt.obstruction: The survey's own weaker conditions (EKFR, C_log, C_log-log) are not of the pointwise form |Im psi| <= g(Re psi): they involve, for each finite measure of finite 1-energy, an integral over the level sets of B = 1 + Re psi against |Fourier transform of mu|^2 and a measure-dependent sequence y_k. Adding exponents moves those level sets, and no relation between the sequences for psi_X, psi_Y and one for psi is available. So the residual open case is exactly the pair where at least one summand satisfies (H) only through a measure-dependent condition.
attempt.key_identity: For independent summands Re psi adds and |Im psi| is subadditive, so every sufficient condition for (H) of the pointwise form |Im psi| <= (1 + Re psi) f(1 + Re psi) with f increasing is closed under independent sums, up to replacing f by 2f.

title: Hunt's hypothesis from coordinate-axis projections
statement: If the one-dimensional projection process of an R^n-valued Levy process X on each coordinate axis satisfies Hunt's hypothesis (H), does X satisfy (H)?
resolved_by: Answered NEGATIVELY inside the source itself. The survey's Section 3.2.1 is headed 'Counterexample for Question 3' and opens: 'We use a counterexample to show that the answer to Question 3 is negative.' The counterexample (PDF p. 16) takes Q = [[2,2],[2,2]], so that sqrt(Q) = [[1,1],[1,1]] and sqrt(Q) R^2 = {(x,y) : x = y}, and a = (1,-1)^T, and sets X_t = a t + sqrt(Q) B_t. Each coordinate-axis projection has a nondegenerate Gaussian part and so satisfies (H) by the survey's Theorem 2.5; the projection on {(x,y) : y = -x} is a uniform motion, which does not satisfy (H); hence X does not satisfy (H) by the survey's Lemma 3.1. Recorded here as an exclusion so that the check is on the record: the objects match by name (the question and the counterexample both concern the coordinate-axis projections of an R^n-valued Levy process), and no external citation is involved.
status_search: No external search needed: the source resolves its own Question 3 two paragraphs after posing it. Recorded as an exclusion rather than silently dropped, so that a merger can see the check.
